key_terms.meaning: x₀ is an ordinary point of y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = 0 when P and Q are both analytic at x₀
x₀ where P or Q blows up but (x − x₀)P and (x − x₀)²Q both stay finite (analytic) as x → x₀
a singular point that is not regular, so Frobenius method is not guaranteed to work there
the function equals its own Taylor series about x₀ in some open interval containing x₀
the equation linking aₙ₊₂ (or aₙ₊₁) to earlier coefficients, got by setting the coefficient of each power of (x − x₀) to zero
Σ aₙ(x − x₀)ⁿ converges for |x − x₀| < R and diverges for |x − x₀| > R; R is at least the distance to the nearest singular point
y = (x − x₀)^r Σ aₙ(x − x₀)ⁿ with a₀ ≠ 0, tried at a regular singular point x₀
r(r − 1) + p₀r + q₀ = 0, where p₀ = lim (x − x₀)P and q₀ = lim (x − x₀)²Q; its roots r₁, r₂ are the possible exponents
(1 − x²)y″ − 2xy′ + n(n + 1)y = 0, which has regular singular points at x = ±1
the polynomial solution of Legendre's equation for integer n ≥ 0, scaled so that Pₙ(1) = 1
Pₙ(x) = (1/(2ⁿ n!)) (dⁿ/dxⁿ)(x² − 1)ⁿ, a closed form for the Legendre polynomial
x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − ν²)y = 0, with a regular singular point at x = 0
J<sub>ν</sub>(x) = Σ<sub>m≥0</sub> (−1)ᵐ (x/2)<sup>2m+ν</sup> / (m! Γ(m + ν + 1)), the Frobenius solution finite at x = 0
Γ(ν) = ∫₀^∞ e<sup>−t</sup> t<sup>ν−1</sup> dt, with Γ(ν + 1) = νΓ(ν) and Γ(n + 1) = n! for integer n
(p y′)′ + (q + λw)y = 0 with p > 0 on [a, b], the form in which eigenvalues are real and eigenfunctions orthogonal
the positive function appearing with λ in the Sturm–Liouville equation; orthogonality is measured against it, ∫ y<sub>m</sub> y<sub>n</sub> w dx = 0
orthogonal eigenfunctions rescaled so that ∫ y<sub>m</sub> y<sub>n</sub> w dx equals 1 when m = n and 0 otherwise
W(x) = W(x₀) exp(−∫ P dx) for y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = 0, so the Wronskian is either never zero or identically zero
zeros of two linearly independent solutions of y″ + P y′ + Q y = 0 interlace: exactly one zero of one solution lies between consecutive zeros of the other
if q₂ ≥ q₁, then between two consecutive zeros of any solution of y″ + q₁y = 0 there lies at least one zero of every solution of y″ + q₂y = 0

takeaways: Classify the point before choosing a method: ordinary point needs a plain power series, regular singular point needs a Frobenius series, irregular point is not covered by either.
The series solution about an ordinary point converges at least out to the nearest singular point of the equation.
The indicial equation r(r − 1) + p₀r + q₀ = 0 gives the exponents; when the two roots differ by an integer or are equal, the second solution usually carries a log term.
Legendre's equation has polynomial solutions only when the separation constant is n(n + 1) with n a whole number, and these Pₙ are orthogonal on [−1, 1] with weight 1.
Bessel's equation gives J<sub>ν</sub>, which is finite at x = 0; J<sub>−ν</sub> gives a second independent solution unless ν is an integer.
Multiplying a second-order linear ODE by an integrating factor always brings it to self-adjoint Sturm–Liouville form, which is what makes orthogonality work.
Abel's formula delivers the Wronskian up to one constant, without solving the equation at all.
Larger q in y″ + q(x)y = 0 makes solutions oscillate faster, and zeros of independent solutions interlace.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always ask for a complete series solution with the recurrence relation and the general solution, or for a Sturm–Liouville and Sturm-theorem argument written out with the orthogonality proof; Legendre and Bessel properties are carried as standard results to be quoted and then used.

bank.q: For y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = 0 define ordinary point, regular singular point and irregular singular point. Classify every point of (a) x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − 4)y = 0, (b) (1 − x²)y″ − 2xy′ + 6y = 0, (c) x³y″ + y = 0.
outline: Write P and Q in standard form and test analyticity at each point
Use the limits p₀ = lim (x − x₀)P and q₀ = lim (x − x₀)²Q to test regularity
(a) x = 0 is regular singular, every other point ordinary
(b) x = ±1 are regular singular points
(c) Q = 1/x³ gives x²Q = 1/x, not analytic, so x = 0 is irregular singular

bank.q: State the theorem guaranteeing a power series solution about an ordinary point of a second-order linear ODE, and explain how the radius of convergence of that series is fixed.
outline: Statement: if x₀ is ordinary, two independent solutions exist as power series in (x − x₀)
Radius of convergence is at least the distance from x₀ to the nearest singular point, real or complex
Illustrate with Legendre's equation about x = 0, where the nearest singular points ±1 force R ≥ 1
Mention that equality can occur and that singular points can be complex, as in (1 + x²)y″ + y = 0

bank.q: Explain the three cases of the roots of the indicial equation and the form the second independent solution takes in each case. Illustrate with Bessel's equation when ν is an integer.
outline: Roots r₁, r₂ with r₁ − r₂ not an integer: two independent Frobenius series
Equal roots: second solution contains a log(x − x₀) term
Roots differing by an integer: second solution may or may not need a log term depending on the coefficients
Bessel with integer ν: J<sub>ν</sub> and J<sub>−ν</sub> are dependent, and Y<sub>ν</sub> supplies the log-type second solution

bank.q: Solve y″ − xy = 0 about x = 0 by the power series method. Find the recurrence, write the two independent solutions and state the radius of convergence.
outline: Assume y = Σ aₙxⁿ and shift indices to a common power
Coefficient of xⁿ gives a<sub>n+2</sub> = a<sub>n−1</sub>/((n + 2)(n + 1)) for n ≥ 1, with a₂ = 0
Write y₁ from a₀ and y₂ from a₁ and list the first four terms of each
No finite singular point, so the series converge for all x

bank.q: Use the Frobenius method to solve 4x y″ + 2y′ + y = 0 about x = 0, stating the indicial equation and the two independent solutions.
outline: Check x = 0 is regular singular
Substitute y = Σ aₙ x<sup>n+r</sup> and collect the lowest power to get 2r(2r − 1) = 0, so r = 0 and r = 1/2
Recurrence a<sub>n+1</sub> = −aₙ / [(n + r + 1)(4(n + r) + 2)]
Write the two series, one for each root, and the general solution as a linear combination

bank.q: Solve Legendre's equation (1 − x²)y″ − 2xy′ + n(n + 1)y = 0 by a power series about x = 0. Show that a polynomial solution appears only for integer n and write P₀, P₁, P₂, P₃.
outline: Assume y = Σ aₖ xᵏ and derive the recurrence a<sub>k+2</sub> = −[(n − k)(n + k + 1)/((k + 2)(k + 1))] aₖ
For integer n one of the two series terminates at k = n and the other does not
Normalize so that Pₙ(1) = 1 and list P₀ = 1, P₁ = x, P₂ = (3x² − 1)/2, P₃ = (5x³ − 3x)/2
Note the regular singular points at x = ±1 bound the interval of validity

bank.q: State the orthogonality relation of Legendre polynomials with its normalization value, and expand f(x) = x² on [−1, 1] in a Legendre series.
outline: Quote ∫<sub>−1</sub><sup>1</sup> P<sub>m</sub>(x) P<sub>n</sub>(x) dx = 0 for m ≠ n and 2/(2n + 1) for m = n
Use coefficients cₙ = ((2n + 1)/2) ∫<sub>−1</sub><sup>1</sup> f(x) Pₙ(x) dx
Only c₀ and c₂ survive by parity, giving x² = (1/3)P₀ + (2/3)P₂
Verify by expanding back to x²

bank.q: Derive the Frobenius series solution of Bessel's equation x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − ν²)y = 0 and hence obtain J<sub>ν</sub>(x). Use it to write J<sub>1/2</sub>(x) and J<sub>−1/2</sub>(x).
outline: Substitute the Frobenius series and get the indicial equation r² − ν² = 0, roots ±ν
Recurrence a<sub>m</sub> = −a<sub>m−2</sub> / ((m + r)² − ν²), odd coefficients vanish
Choose a₀ = 1/(2<sup>ν</sup> Γ(ν + 1)) and produce the standard series for J<sub>ν</sub>
Use Γ(3/2) = √π/2 to obtain J<sub>1/2</sub> = √(2/(πx)) sin x and J<sub>−1/2</sub> = √(2/(πx)) cos x

bank.q: Expand a function f(x) on [0, 1] in a series of Bessel functions J<sub>n</sub>(α<sub>k</sub>x), where α<sub>k</sub> are the positive zeros of J<sub>n</sub>. State the coefficient formula and the weight.
outline: Use the orthogonality ∫₀<sup>1</sup> x J<sub>n</sub>(α<sub>j</sub>x) J<sub>n</sub>(α<sub>k</sub>x) dx = 0 for j ≠ k
Coefficient c<sub>k</sub> = [2 / J<sub>n+1</sub>(α<sub>k</sub>)²] ∫₀<sup>1</sup> x f(x) J<sub>n</sub>(α<sub>k</sub>x) dx
The weight is x, coming from Bessel's equation in self-adjoint form
State the Fourier–Bessel series and note convergence in the mean

bank.q: Put a₂(x)y″ + a₁(x)y′ + (a₀(x) + λ)y = 0 into self-adjoint Sturm–Liouville form. State the Sturm–Liouville theorem and prove that eigenfunctions belonging to different eigenvalues are orthogonal with weight w.
outline: Divide by a₂ and multiply by the integrating factor exp(∫ a₁/a₂ dx)
Identify p, q and w explicitly and state the boundary conditions
State reality of eigenvalues, orthogonality of eigenfunctions, and completeness
Proof: multiply each equation by the other eigenfunction, subtract, integrate, and use Green's identity with the boundary terms vanishing

bank.q: Express Legendre's equation and Bessel's equation in self-adjoint form, read off p, q and w in each case, and use this to explain why the weights are 1 and x in their orthogonality relations.
outline: Legendre: ((1 − x²)y′)′ + n(n + 1)y = 0, so p = 1 − x², w = 1, singular endpoints at ±1
Bessel: (x y′)′ + (x − ν²/x)y = 0, so p = x, w = x
Apply the Lagrange identity to get ∫ (P<sub>m</sub>P<sub>n</sub>) dx = 0 and ∫ x J<sub>ν</sub>(αx) J<sub>ν</sub>(βx) dx = 0
Note the polynomial case terminates so no endpoint condition is needed for Legendre

bank.q: State and prove Abel's formula for the Wronskian of y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = 0. Apply it to show that W(cos x, sin x) is a nonzero constant.
outline: Write W = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂ and differentiate
Use the ODE to replace each y″ and cancel terms to get W′ = −P W
Solve the first-order equation to get W = W₀ exp(−∫ P dx)
Consequence: W is either never zero or identically zero, which is the linear independence test
For y″ + y = 0, P = 0, so W is constant and equals 1

bank.q: State the Sturm separation theorem and prove that the zeros of two linearly independent solutions of a second-order linear ODE interlace.
outline: State the theorem precisely, including that the ODE is in the form y″ + P y′ + Q y = 0
Take consecutive zeros x₁ < x₂ of y₁ and suppose y₂ has no zero in between
Apply Rolle-type reasoning to the Wronskian, whose sign must change inside (x₁, x₂) yet is fixed by Abel's formula
Conclude a contradiction, so y₂ has exactly one zero in (x₁, x₂)

bank.q: State the Sturm comparison theorem. Use it to show that every solution of y″ + (1 + x²)y = 0 has infinitely many zeros, and compare the spacing of zeros with those of y″ + y = 0.
outline: State both theorems clearly with the condition q₂ ≥ q₁
Compare q₂ = 1 + x² with q₁ = 1, so 1 + x² ≥ 1 everywhere
Between consecutive zeros of cos x or sin x there is a zero of every solution of the comparison equation
Zeros of the comparison equation are π apart, so the solution of the given equation has zeros spaced at most π apart on the whole line

bank.q: Compare the power series method and the Frobenius method: when each applies, what form of solution is assumed, how the index is found, and what happens in the exceptional cases of the indicial roots.
outline: Ordinary point: plain power series, index fixed at n ≥ 0, always two solutions
Regular singular point: Frobenius series, index r from the indicial equation
Three root cases and the role of the log term in the second solution
Radius of convergence still governed by the nearest singular point
Give one worked equation of each type as illustration

glossary.def: A function that can be written as a convergent Taylor series in a neighbourhood of the point in question.
A point where both coefficient functions P and Q of the standard-form second-order linear ODE are analytic.
A point where P or Q fails to be analytic, so the equation cannot be treated by a plain power series there.
A singular point at which (x − x₀)P and (x − x₀)²Q stay analytic, so the Frobenius method applies.
A singular point at which those limits fail to exist or fail to be analytic.
An infinite sum Σ aₙ(x − x₀)ⁿ which converges inside some interval or disc around x₀.
The number R such that the series converges absolutely for |x − x₀| < R and diverges outside.
A formula expressing each new coefficient of the series in terms of earlier ones.
The technique of seeking a solution in the form (x − x₀)^r Σ aₙ(x − x₀)ⁿ at a regular singular point.
The quadratic in r obtained from the lowest power of x after substitution; its roots are the exponents of the Frobenius solutions.
The extension of the factorial to non-integers, defined by an integral and satisfying Γ(ν + 1) = νΓ(ν).
The ODE (1 − x²)y″ − 2xy′ + n(n + 1)y = 0, arising from problems with spherical symmetry.
The terminating polynomial solution Pₙ of Legendre's equation with n a non-negative integer, normalized by Pₙ(1) = 1.
The derivative formula Pₙ(x) = (1/(2ⁿ n!)) (dⁿ/dxⁿ)(x² − 1)ⁿ for the Legendre polynomial.
The ODE x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − ν²)y = 0, arising in circular and cylindrical problems.

glossary.term: Bessel function of the first kind
glossary.def: The solution J<sub>ν</sub> of Bessel's equation that stays finite at x = 0, given by a Frobenius series.

glossary.term: Bessel function of the second kind
glossary.def: The independent partner Y<sub>ν</sub>, which blows up at x = 0 and carries a logarithmic term when ν is an integer.
A family of functions whose products integrate to zero against a weight whenever the indices differ.
The positive multiplier w(x) inside the orthogonality integral for a Sturm–Liouville problem.
A value of the parameter λ for which the boundary value problem has a nonzero solution.
The nonzero solution of the boundary value problem belonging to a particular eigenvalue.
A second-order linear ODE written as (p y′)′ + q y = 0, so that Lagrange's identity and orthogonality follow directly.
The determinant W = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂, which is nonzero exactly when the two solutions are linearly independent.
The statement that the Wronskian of two solutions of y″ + P y′ + Q y = 0 equals a constant times exp(−∫ P dx).
Two linearly independent solutions of the same second-order linear ODE have interlacing zeros.
A larger coefficient q(x) forces faster oscillation, so zeros appear more often.
